The creature is called a **veilback**, and at first glance it looks like a piece of night sky drifting beneath the sea.

It lives on a cold planet where liquid ammonia fills the ocean basins. Under a dense atmosphere, the seas remain fluid at temperatures far below the freezing point of water. Their surface is dark and restless, reflecting a small orange sun. Along the shores, water ice forms cliffs as solid and enduring as granite.

### Appearance

An adult veilback is about three meters long, but most of that length is an almost transparent mantle: six broad, overlapping fins surrounding a narrow central body. When it swims, the fins ripple in sequence, making it resemble a translucent flower slowly turning inside out.

Its tissues have a smoky violet tint. Branching through them are silver-white channels that carry dissolved nutrients and reactive chemicals. These channels gather around three dark organs near the center of its body, giving the impression of a constellation seen through cloud.

It has no head in the familiar sense. A ring of short, jointed feelers surrounds a feeding slit on its underside. Each feeler ends in a fan of delicate filaments, usually folded away like a closed umbrella.

The upper surface is studded with flat, charcoal-colored plates. They protect the soft mantle from floating ice fragments and from the hooked feeding limbs of predators. Between the plates, faint blue lights blink.

### A body built for ammonia

The veilback does not contain blood, fat, and muscle as Earth animals do. Its internal fluid is ammonia rich in dissolved salts, and its cells—or their equivalents—are enclosed by chemically resistant molecular films.

Its biochemistry would have to be radically different from ours. In this imagined ecosystem, flexible nitrogen-rich molecules perform some of the jobs that proteins do on Earth, while layered membranes keep incompatible reactions apart.

Cold makes most of its chemistry slow. A veilback may take several minutes to fold itself around a meal, and a wound can require years to close. Yet it is not always sluggish: elastic fibers store energy gradually, then release it in a sudden snap. A threatened animal can vanish into the dark with one violent contraction of its mantle.

That escape is expensive. Afterward, it may remain nearly motionless for days.

### How it feeds

Veilbacks graze on **chemical reefs** around seafloor fissures.

These reefs are living crusts of microorganisms that exploit chemical differences between material rising from the planet’s interior and substances dissolved in the ocean. They grow in wrinkled black sheets over pale mineral chimneys.

The veilback settles over a patch and opens its feeding fans. Thousands of filaments comb the reef, loosening flakes and drawing them toward its mouth. It also cultivates some of these microorganisms inside sheltered folds of its mantle. Their waste products supplement its diet; in return, they receive a steady flow of useful chemicals.

A well-fed veilback carries a dark, velvety garden beneath its fins.

### Senses and behavior

Vision is useful only near the surface. In deeper water, the veilback reads its surroundings through vibration and chemistry.

Its mantle detects pressure waves from moving animals. Its feelers distinguish faint chemical trails, allowing it to locate a reef—or recognize a familiar individual—long before contact.

The blue lights along its back serve as close-range signals. A slow traveling pulse means *occupied feeding ground*. Three brief flashes invite another veilback to approach. During courtship, two animals hover edge to edge and synchronize their lights, sometimes for several days.

They often travel in loose groups. When one finds a rich reef, chemicals released from its mantle draw the others toward it. From above, the gathering looks like a bed of dim lanterns opening on the ocean floor.

### Life cycle

Young veilbacks begin as grain-sized capsules attached beneath an adult’s protective plates. They remain there through their earliest development, nourished by secretions from the parent’s microbial garden.

Eventually they detach and rise into the upper ocean, where currents disperse them. Most never reach a suitable reef.

Those that survive may live for centuries. Old individuals become asymmetrical: a torn fin, a cracked plate, a branching scar that glows differently from the surrounding tissue.

In the ammonia sea, such an animal moves with extraordinary patience—its six veils lifting and falling, its little blue signals passing through the dark, its body carrying the accumulated damage of a very long life.

Instead, a slightly thickened leading edge carries a fringe of sensory filaments, while a trailing cord serves as both rudder and anchor.

Its skin looks like smoky glass. Beneath it, branching channels carry a violet transport fluid, and small reflective plates flicker as the animal moves. These plates are not scales but adjustable shutters: the glassmantle can expose its delicate inner tissues to the weak sunlight or shield them from sudden brightness and chemical irritation.

It swims by sending slow waves around its perimeter. In calm water, the movement is so smooth that it seems to slide without effort. When threatened, all six ribs contract at once, folding the body into a narrow dart.

### Life in a different solvent

The glassmantle is not an Earth animal with ammonia substituted for blood. Its entire chemistry belongs to another evolutionary history.

Its tissues are built from hypothetical molecular structures that remain flexible and reactive in cold ammonia. Instead of ordinary cell membranes, its microscopic compartments have boundaries suited to that solvent; its catalysts perform the work that enzymes do on Earth, but with different chemical machinery.

Cold makes many reactions sluggish, so the glassmantle lives slowly. A feeding excursion lasts several Earth days. Wounds close over months. An adult may spend a century patrolling the same submerged ridge.

But slow does not mean helpless. Its swimming membranes store elastic energy, allowing a brief, sharp escape even when the chemistry powering it works at a patient pace.

The glassmantle grazes on **velvet reefs**: thick colonies of microorganisms growing where mineral-rich fluids seep through fractures in the icy crust.

Those microbes harvest energy from chemical differences between the seep fluids and the surrounding ocean. The glassmantle settles over a patch like a blanket, seals its rim against the reef, and releases a small amount of digestive fluid into the enclosed space. Thousands of tiny grooves on its underside then draw in the loosened nutrients.

A feeding glassmantle slowly darkens from transparent gray to bruised purple.

It must be careful around the seeps. Warmth accelerates its metabolism, but too much damages its tissues. Juveniles sometimes misjudge that boundary; old individuals bear cloudy scars where their membranes were injured.

Instead, its rim contains dozens of light-sensitive patches that register brightness and movement. Chemical receptors taste passing currents, detecting food, predators, and the lingering traces of other glassmantles. Fine sensory hairs map pressure changes, allowing it to feel a large swimmer approaching through the darkness.

Its most distinctive sense is electrical. At close range, sensitive organs along its ribs detect the faint electrical activity of living tissues. A reef hidden beneath sediment is, to the glassmantle, not silent ground but a field of tiny signals.

An approaching mate is recognizable partly by the rhythm of those signals.

During the long twilight season, adults gather in sheltered shallows. They arrange their reflective plates into shifting bands, turning their bodies into pale, moving mosaics.

Two compatible individuals circle one another for hours, matching the waves of their swimming membranes. Eventually, they touch their trailing cords together and exchange packets of hereditary material.

The survivors spend their first years clinging to reef crevices before becoming broad enough to swim against coastal currents.

If you stood safely behind the window of a submerged habitat, a glassmantle might settle against the glass.

First you would see the violet channels, branching like winter trees. Then the underside would spread across your view: six pale ribs, a lacework of feeding grooves, and hundreds of sensory threads gently testing the unfamiliar surface.

It would not recognize a face on the other side.

### The Veilgrazer

At first glance, it looks like a piece of night caught beneath the ice.

The veilgrazer lives in a shallow ocean of liquid ammonia on a cold, rocky planet. Above it, a dense nitrogen atmosphere carries clouds of ammonia snow. A distant sun appears through the haze as a small amber coin, giving little warmth. Most of the energy that sustains life comes from the planet itself: tides flex its crust, and mineral-rich fluids seep through cracks in the seabed.

In this imagined biology, ammonia serves the role water plays on Earth—the liquid in which the chemistry of life takes place.

**Body and movement**

An adult veilgrazer is about two meters across but only a few centimeters thick. Its body resembles a translucent, six-lobed cloak, with a raised central hub containing its digestive chambers and nerve-like signaling tissues. Dark branching channels spread from the hub to the edges, giving it the appearance of a leaf made from smoked glass.

Its tissues are built from flexible organic compounds suited to temperatures around −60°C. Rather than ordinary terrestrial cell membranes, it has specialized molecular barriers that remain pliable in liquid ammonia.

Along its underside are thousands of short, hooked filaments. These anchor it to the seabed and comb through mineral sediment. When disturbed, it releases its grip and sends a slow ripple around its six lobes. The ripple pushes it forward without stirring much sediment—a useful trait for an animal that survives partly by remaining unnoticed.

Swimming veilgrazers look like umbrellas repeatedly turning themselves inside out.

**Feeding**

The veilgrazer cultivates much of its own food.

The branching channels inside its body house colonies of microscopic organisms. These symbionts draw chemical energy from the disequilibrium between substances carried up from the crust and those dissolved in the surrounding ocean. The veilgrazer supplies fresh fluid and trace minerals; the colonies provide it with energy-rich compounds.

It also grazes on the dark microbial films growing around seabed seeps. Its feeding surface is not a mouth but a broad underside covered with tiny chemical-processing pits. It settles over a patch of film, secretes digestive agents, and absorbs the resulting molecules.

A meal may take several days. Much of its biochemistry runs slowly at these temperatures. After feeding, a veilgrazer can remain nearly motionless for weeks, its edges lifting only enough to refresh the ammonia beneath it.

**Senses**

It has no eyes.

Instead, six sensitive ridges on its upper surface detect changes in pressure, temperature, and dissolved chemicals. Together they let it distinguish the steady seep of a feeding ground from the irregular wake of a swimming predator.

It can also sense weak electric fields at close range. To a veilgrazer, another living creature has an electrical outline: the faint, shifting signature of chemical gradients moving through its body.

Its world is therefore not a landscape of colors but a tapestry of currents, chemical trails, and nearby pulses.

**Defense and communication**

When threatened, the veilgrazer contracts into a thick, folded knot, protecting its delicate feeding surface. Brittle mineral plates embedded in its upper skin overlap as it folds, creating a rough little shield.

If seized, it can shed one of its lobes. The detached section continues contracting, distracting the attacker while the rest escapes. Regrowth is slow.

During breeding periods, adults gather around warm seeps and exchange low-frequency vibrations through the rock. A human instrument would register these signals as long, overlapping tremors. Each individual’s rhythm reflects its size and condition.

**Young**

Its offspring begin life inside tough, amber-colored capsules attached to porous stones. Each capsule contains both an embryo and a small starter colony of its parent’s symbiotic microbes.

The young emerge no larger than a fingernail, with only three lobes. They spend their first years hidden in cracks, gradually developing the remaining three.

A mature veilgrazer may live for centuries. Around a dependable seep, generations accumulate in overlapping rings, their translucent bodies gently rising and falling in the current—a cold, patient reef beneath an ammonia sea.

### The Lantern Skate

Beneath a lavender sky, where liquid-ammonia waves break against black volcanic shores, the lantern skate moves like a piece of night that has learned to swim.

It is roughly two meters across, broad and almost paper-thin at its edges. Six flexible fins surround a low central body, their slow, overlapping ripples carrying it through the sea without a splash. From above, its skin is matte charcoal, dusted with reflective flecks. From below, it glows a faint green, matching the dim light filtering down from the sky.

Its world is bitterly cold by human standards. The open oceans hover near −50°C, kept liquid by the planet’s climate and atmospheric pressure. Water is not the substance of life here: it is a mineral, locked into cliffs, buried glaciers, and pale pebbles on the seabed.

The lantern skate has never encountered a warm rain.

### A body built for ammonia

The skate has no bones. A flexible internal lattice supports its body, strong around the central organs and delicate within the fins. Its tissues resemble layered gel rather than meat, enclosed by tough, chemically resistant membranes.

Its biochemistry would be unfamiliar to us. Instead of water, liquid ammonia carries dissolved substances through its cells. Its molecular machinery is adapted to a solvent that behaves differently from water, using bonds and folded structures that would not necessarily survive inside an Earth organism.

At these temperatures, chemistry proceeds slowly. So does the skate.

A single contraction of its central pumping organ takes almost a minute. Meals may sustain it for weeks. When food becomes scarce, it settles into a hollow in the seabed and reduces its activity until it seems less like an animal than a discarded sheet of leather.

What looks like sluggishness is economy. Sudden movement is expensive, and there are few reasons to hurry in a cold sea.

### How it senses the world

Around the rim of its body runs a fringe of translucent filaments. These taste dissolved chemicals, registering the faint trails left by prey and the changing chemistry near volcanic vents.

The skate’s eyes are small, dark pits on its upper surface. They distinguish movement and brightness but little detail. Its most useful sense is spread across its underside: arrays of sensitive receptors detect weak electrical disturbances nearby.

A buried animal flexing beneath the sediment appears to the skate as a brief, localized flicker.

Its green light comes from slow chemical reactions in sealed pockets beneath the skin. By opening or closing opaque layers over these pockets, it can display moving bands, spots, and branching lines. Two skates meeting in deep water exchange patterns over several minutes before deciding whether to approach.

A mating display may last three days.

### Feeding at the cold gardens

Lantern skates gather around “cold gardens”: broad mats of microscopic life growing where mineral-rich fluids seep through the seabed. The seepage is warmer than the surrounding ocean, but not hot enough to boil it away. Chemical imbalances between the fluids and seawater provide energy for the garden’s inhabitants.

The skate eats both the mats and the small grazers living among them.

Its mouth is a soft slit underneath its central body. It lands over a patch of food, seals its fin edges against the ground, and releases a small quantity of digestive fluid into the enclosed space. Hours later, it draws the resulting slurry inward.

Older skates cultivate gardens of their own. Grooves along their backs shelter colonies of microbes, supplied with waste products from the animal. During lean periods, the skate harvests part of this living coat with specialized grooming tendrils.

A well-fed adult looks faintly mossy.

### Young that travel like seeds

Once in its long reproductive cycle, a skate anchors itself beneath a rocky shelf and produces a cluster of translucent capsules. Each contains a miniature juvenile wrapped around a packet of stored nutrients.

The capsules detach gradually. Small gas-filled chambers keep them suspended, allowing currents to carry them far from their parent.

For months they drift through the dim upper ocean.

When a capsule encounters the chemical signature of a suitable seabed garden, its buoyancy chamber slowly collapses. It sinks, catches among the rocks, and splits open. A skate no larger than a fingernail unfolds six nearly invisible fins.

An adult may live for centuries, provided the ocean remains cold.

### Its greatest danger

The lantern skate fears warmth more than darkness.

An unusually vigorous eruption can send a lethal plume across the seabed, disrupting its delicate chemistry and filling the water with expanding bubbles. Its first response is to fold two fins beneath itself and flee on the other four, abandoning the graceful symmetry of ordinary swimming.

Afterward, survivors settle at the edge of the devastated gardens. Their lights remain shuttered while new microbial films slowly cover the bare rock.

To a human observer, nothing would seem to happen.

Then, several hours later, one skate would lift its edge and begin to feed.

### The Glassmantle

From the shore, it looks like a patch of ocean that has decided to move against the current.

The glassmantle lives in the shallow ammonia seas of a cold, rocky planet beneath a dim red sun. The beaches are dark volcanic grit, and the “ice” forming pale cliffs along the coast is mostly frozen water—as solid and enduring here as limestone on Earth.

The creature is about three meters across, broad and low, with six rippling fins arranged around a central body. It has no obvious head. Instead, a slightly raised ridge marks its forward edge, giving it the silhouette of a translucent kite.

**Its body is a window full of weather.**

The glassmantle’s outer skin is clear, tough, and faintly amber. Beneath it, branching channels carry a dark violet fluid. Slow contractions push this fluid through the body in traveling pulses, so a resting animal seems to contain a distant lightning storm.

Its imagined biochemistry uses liquid ammonia as a solvent rather than water. Flexible carbon-based molecules form its tissues, but their structures and reaction pathways differ radically from those of terrestrial life. At such low temperatures, chemical reactions tend to proceed slowly; the glassmantle compensates with specialized catalysts, extensive internal exchange surfaces, and a patient way of living.

A single sweep of its fins takes several seconds. Digestion can take weeks. An adult may live for centuries.

**It grazes on chemical gardens.**

Along cracks in the seabed, comparatively warm fluids seep out of the crust, carrying dissolved minerals. These feed thick, rust-colored mats of ammonia-adapted microorganisms. The glassmantle settles over a mat and presses its underside against the rock.

There, thousands of tiny flexible teeth work like a living rasp.

The loosened material enters a ring-shaped digestive chamber, where resident microbes help break it down. Other tissues store energy-rich compounds and complementary reactants obtained from different parts of the sea. Moving between those chemical environments is as essential to the glassmantle as breathing is to us.

Its metabolism produces a little heat, but it does not keep an Earth-warm interior. That would be ruinously expensive—and could boil the solvent on which its tissues depend.

**It sees with its edges.**

Around the rim of the body are dozens of small, black light-sensitive cups. Together they detect shadows, the direction of the sun, and the dim glimmers of other organisms. They cannot form a sharp picture.

For close navigation, the glassmantle relies on vibration and chemistry. Fine filaments trailing beneath its fins taste the currents. A feeding ground upstream arrives first as a faint chemical signature, then as a widening trail that the animal follows across the seabed.

It recognizes others of its kind through patterned pulses of violet light beneath the skin. A greeting can take half an hour.

**When threatened, it becomes difficult to hold.**

Its principal predators are narrow, jointed animals that probe beneath its mantle. In response, the glassmantle clamps its rim against the seabed and stiffens its skin into a shallow dome.

If dislodged, it ejects a cloud of dark, plate-shaped crystals and folds its six fins backward. One powerful contraction sends it gliding away, leaving a glittering false silhouette slowly dispersing in its wake.

**Its young begin as drifting lanterns.**

Once every few decades, adults gather above warm coastal seeps and release translucent reproductive capsules. The developing young float near the surface, sustained by stored nutrients and light-harvesting symbionts.

For several years, they resemble tiny amber bells.

Eventually, they grow heavy enough to sink. Most vanish into the dark. A few reach the mineral gardens, spread their six small fins, and begin the long, slow work of becoming an almost invisible giant.

At first, it looks like a piece of night sky caught beneath the ice: a dark, translucent shape scattered with green points of light. Then its edges unfold, and something as broad as a dining table glides through the ammonia sea.

The **lantern-sail** lives on a cold planet orbiting a dim red star. Here, the oceans remain liquid at roughly −50°C, beneath a dense atmosphere of nitrogen, hydrogen, and ammonia vapor. Water exists mostly as rock-hard ice. Along the coast, cliffs of frozen water descend into pale, pungent seas.

Its biology would be speculative—but it might work very differently from anything on Earth.

#### A body built like a living kite

The lantern-sail has no head, spine, or clearly defined front. Its body is a flattened hexagon, about two meters across, with six flexible ribs radiating from a central digestive chamber. Between those ribs stretch thin sheets of dark violet tissue.

Rippling these sheets propels it through the liquid. In a strong current, it folds into a narrow dart; in still water, it spreads wide and drifts, making tiny adjustments with its curled tips.

Its upper surface is covered in overlapping, translucent plates of tough organic material. These protect it from floating crystals and small predators without making it rigid. Beneath them lies a honeycomb of fluid-filled chambers. By changing the composition and density of the fluid inside, it can rise or sink without constant swimming.

Viewed from below, it resembles a stained-glass window: branching channels, cloudy internal organs, and little lights burning at the ends of its ribs.

#### Chemistry without water

Inside the lantern-sail, liquid ammonia plays the role that water plays in terrestrial cells. It carries dissolved substances, supports chemical reactions, and transports waste.

Its tissues would not simply be Earth flesh chilled to an impossible temperature. Its cell boundaries would need to be made from compounds that remain flexible in ammonia, and its catalysts would have to function in a cold solvent with very different chemical properties. Its hereditary material might be an unfamiliar information-bearing polymer rather than DNA.

Even with such adaptations, it lives slowly.

A swimming stroke takes several seconds. Digesting a substantial meal can take weeks. When food becomes scarce, the creature folds its membranes around its central chamber and enters a near-motionless state, surviving on stored chemical energy for months.

What looks like sluggishness to a human observer is normal life at the pace of this ocean.

#### Feeding beneath the frozen cliffs

The lantern-sail grazes on dense colonies of microscopic organisms growing where mineral-rich seepage enters the sea. These colonies exploit chemical imbalances between material rising from the planet’s interior and reactive substances delivered from the atmosphere.

To feed, the creature settles over a patch of growth and seals its edges against the surface. Hundreds of fine, retractable filaments emerge from its underside. They loosen the colony and draw the fragments into a central opening.

It is not entirely peaceful. If a smaller swimmer becomes trapped beneath its feeding canopy, the lantern-sail will digest that too.

Old individuals often carry gardens of harmless microbes in the grooves between their armor plates. Their backs appear dusted with black velvet.

#### Seeing with its whole edge

Six clusters of light-sensitive organs sit at the tips of its ribs. They cannot form sharp images, but together they detect movement, brightness, and the direction of the faint sunlight filtering through the sea.

More important are chemical sensors along its margins. A lantern-sail can follow a plume of dissolved nutrients or detect the waste products of a predator long before it comes into view.

Its green lights are produced by a hypothetical low-temperature chemical reaction. Usually, they are almost imperceptible. During courtship, however, the six tips brighten in a slow, repeating sequence.

A potential mate answers with its own pattern. Their exchange can continue for hours before they touch.

#### Young that ride the currents

After mating, both individuals release clusters of tiny, armored young. Each juvenile resembles a closed umbrella and trails a long filament that catches currents.

For the first part of its life, it drifts near the surface, feeding on suspended microbes. Only when its six ribs become strong enough does it descend toward the coastal feeding grounds.

Most never reach them.

Those that do may live for centuries, their armor accumulating scars and mineral stains. In the oldest lantern-sails, the violet membranes fade almost to transparency.

From above, you could look straight through one into the dark sea below—until six green lights slowly awakened around its edge.

The sea around it remains near −60°C, cold enough that ordinary Earth organisms would freeze solid. Here, however, liquid ammonia fills the role that water plays in terrestrial life: carrying dissolved substances, allowing chemical reactions, and circulating nutrients.

The glassmantle’s chemistry would have to be profoundly different from ours. Its tissues are built from imagined ammonia-compatible polymers—flexible molecular chains that remain supple in the cold. Instead of a watery cell interior enclosed in familiar fatty membranes, it has microscopic compartments bounded by tough, chemically resistant films.

Its outer surface resembles smoked glass. Embedded mineral flakes strengthen the skin without making it rigid, so the animal can fold almost in half when a current catches it.

Around its edge hangs a fringe of hundreds of fine tendrils. In still conditions they spread outward, giving it the appearance of a pale, many-pointed star.

A traveling ripple passes around the glassmantle’s rim, slowly pushing it through the sea. It seldom moves faster than a human walking.

When threatened, it draws its fringe inward and contracts a ring of muscular tissue around its underside. Ammonia shoots from a rear-facing siphon, propelling the creature several body lengths backward. The escape leaves a cloud of glittering, discarded skin flakes.

The glassmantle grazes where mineral-rich fluids seep through cracks in the seabed.

Light penetrates only the upper layers of the sea, so sight is secondary. Small light-sensitive patches along its rim distinguish brightness, movement, and the looming shadow of a hunter.

In the shallow ammonia seas of a cold, cloud-wrapped planet, the lantern veil drifts like a torn piece of illuminated silk.

Long feeding threads trail from the canopy’s edges. When threatened, it draws those threads inward and folds into a compact, leathery bell.

Seen from above, it is almost invisible against the black sea. Seen from below, it glows a faint green.

#### A body built for bitter cold

The lantern veil inhabits oceans at around −50°C, beneath a dense atmosphere that helps keep ammonia liquid. Water on this world is mostly a mineral: hard ice forming cliffs, gravel, and much of the seabed.

Its biology is not simply Earth biology with a different fluid substituted. In this imagined ecosystem, evolution has produced flexible, nitrogen-rich structural molecules and membranes that remain stable in liquid ammonia. Its internal fluids are ammonia-based, carrying dissolved nutrients and reactive compounds between tissues.

The creature feels less like jelly than like thin silicone rubber. Its outer skin has several layers: a tough, nearly transparent sheath; a mesh of contractile fibers; and an inner chemical barrier that carefully regulates what enters its body.

Life moves slowly here. A damaged canopy may take years to regrow. A mature lantern veil might live for several centuries, spending much of that time almost motionless.

#### How it moves

Six muscular ribs radiate from the central organ mass. By bending them in sequence, the creature sends a ripple around its canopy, pushing itself through the sea with a smooth, corkscrewing motion.

It rarely swims against a current. Instead, it adjusts its shape to ride one layer of moving liquid while allowing its feeding threads to hang into another. This lets it sweep a large volume of ocean while using very little energy.

During storms, lantern veils descend toward the seabed and anchor themselves with hooked tips hidden inside their feeding threads. Entire colonies can settle over a ridge of water ice, their folded bodies resembling pale flowers pressed flat by wind.

#### What it eats

The foundation of its food web lies near geological seeps, where substances from the planet’s interior meet chemically different compounds in the ocean. Microbial life exploits those reactions for energy, forming dark, slow-growing films on ice and stone.

Tiny grazers feed on these films. The lantern veil catches the grazers.

Its trailing threads bear thousands of microscopic pockets lined with adhesive material. Contact with suitable prey triggers a local contraction, curling the thread around the animal and drawing it toward the underside of the canopy. There, a ring of small digestive chambers breaks the meal down.

Digestion is measured in days, not hours. After a substantial feeding, the central organs darken from smoky violet to almost black.

#### How it senses the world

It has no face and no single brain. A ring of nerve-like tissue coordinates six smaller processing centers, one beneath each lobe.

Along the canopy’s rim are light-sensitive patches that distinguish the dim sky from the darker depths. More important are its chemical senses. The feeding threads detect minute changes in dissolved substances, allowing it to follow the faint plume of a productive seep.

It also senses pressure and vibration. An approaching predator registers first as a disturbance traveling through the canopy: a direction, a rhythm, a growing urgency.

The green light comes from colonies of symbiotic organisms housed in channels beneath its skin. Their glow helps conceal its silhouette from predators looking upward toward the faintly lit surface.

From the shore, it looks like a crack moving through the sea.

The glasswake lives beneath the pale, slow swells of an ammonia ocean, on a planet where the air is thick and the temperature hovers near −55°C. Its world has no rainforests, no coral reefs, no familiar green. Black volcanic islands rise from violet-gray water, and storms drag curtains of frozen ammonia across the horizon.

An adult glasswake is about three meters long, shaped like a broad ribbon with six short limbs tucked beneath it. Its body is almost transparent. Suspended inside are branching silver vessels, clusters of dark organs, and a long central cord that flashes faintly when the animal turns. Seen from above, these structures resemble frost spreading across a window.

Its transparency is camouflage. In the dim light of its planet’s distant sun, a solid silhouette would advertise a meal.

#### A body made for a different solvent

The glasswake has no water-based blood. Its internal fluids are mixtures of liquid ammonia and dissolved compounds, maintained at a composition slightly different from the surrounding ocean.

Its cells would need chemistry unlike ours: flexible molecular barriers that remain stable in ammonia, and catalysts that work at temperatures where terrestrial animals freeze solid. Much of this biochemistry is speculative, but one consequence shapes the entire creature: **it lives slowly**.

A resting glasswake may take several minutes to complete the equivalent of a breath. Small injuries seal over days. A well-fed adult can go months between substantial meals.

Its outer skin is a flexible composite reinforced with microscopic mineral plates. These overlap rather than fuse, allowing it to bend without cracking in the cold. Along its sides run thin, frilled folds that exchange dissolved substances with the sea.

#### How it finds its way

The glasswake has no recognizable face.

At its leading edge, a crescent of dark sensory tissue detects light and movement. Beneath that crescent hang two delicate combs, each carrying hundreds of filaments. These taste chemical trails and register disturbances in the ocean’s electric field.

To a glasswake, a nearby animal is not primarily a shape. It is a moving electrical presence surrounded by a plume of chemistry.

Its six limbs end in spreading fans. In open water, the creature swims by sending slow waves down its body. On the seafloor, it walks with extraordinary care, placing each fan against the sediment before shifting its weight.

#### Feeding at the warm places

Most glasswakes gather around volcanic seep fields, where chemical-rich fluids sustain mats of alien microbial life.

They graze by laying their undersides over these mats. A soft feeding membrane unfolds, secretes digestive compounds, and draws in the products. Occasionally, a glasswake traps a smaller grazer beneath its body, wrapping around it like a transparent blanket.

The volcanic fields are also dangerous. A fresh eruption can heat the local ocean enough to make it boil. Glasswakes detect approaching changes in temperature and chemistry, then retreat in long, nearly silent processions.

#### The silver nursery

Once every few decades, adults migrate into shallow basins and anchor themselves side by side. They release translucent capsules that cling to the undersides of mineral shelves.

Each capsule contains a developing juvenile and a starter colony of symbiotic microbes. The young depend on those microbes to process their first meals.

Newly hatched glasswakes are opaque white, no larger than a human finger. For years, they hide among branching mineral deposits before becoming transparent enough to venture into open water.

An adult might live for centuries.

If you stood safely above its ocean, you could watch one pass beneath your feet: a ripple, a glimmer of silver anatomy, six limbs folding inward. Then the sea would appear empty again.

Lantern sieves gather near volcanic seep fields, where warmer, chemically enriched fluid escapes through cracks in the seafloor. These places are the planet’s equivalent of fertile valleys.

CREATURE DESCRIPTION:
The first thing you would notice is that it seems to be swimming upside down.

Its body hangs beneath a broad, translucent fan, with six ribbonlike limbs trailing into the dark. When the fan contracts, the creature rises through the ammonia ocean in a slow, soundless pulse. When it relaxes, it drifts downward, gathering food on the fine branches of its limbs.

Human explorers call it a **glassmantle**.

### Its world

The glassmantle lives on a cold planet beneath a thick, oxygen-poor atmosphere. At the ocean’s surface, temperatures hover around −50°C—warm enough for liquid ammonia under the local conditions, but lethally cold to most Earth life. Dissolved salts and other compounds make the sea cloudy and electrically conductive.

The sky is copper-colored with photochemical haze. A small, dim sun appears through it as a blurred red disk. Storms drive pale waves against black volcanic shores.

Ammonia is not simply colder water: it dissolves substances differently and would demand unfamiliar biological chemistry. The glassmantle’s cells, catalysts, and hereditary molecules would therefore have to be fundamentally unlike ours.

### A body like smoked glass

An adult is about two meters across, though most of that width is delicate feeding tissue. Its central body is a flattened spindle suspended beneath the swimming fan.

The outer covering resembles flexible, smoky quartz. It is actually a layered organic composite: tough fibers embedded in a material that remains supple at temperatures where rubber would stiffen. Beneath it, branching channels circulate a dark violet fluid.

There are no bones. Internal pressure supports the body, while overlapping bands of contractile tissue alter its shape. When threatened, the glassmantle folds its fan tightly around its central organs and becomes a compact, ridged package that sinks rapidly.

Along its underside are rows of silver-gray nodules. These contain mineral grains collected from food and used as adjustable ballast. Young animals are nearly transparent; old ones carry so much mineral material that their undersides resemble tarnished jewelry.

### Eating the ocean’s chemistry

The glassmantle grazes where warm, mineral-rich seep water mixes with the colder ocean—not water in the terrestrial sense, but circulating ammonia laden with dissolved compounds.

Its ribbons carry thousands of microscopic cups. These capture drifting colonies of native microorganisms and flakes of organic matter. Periodically, a ribbon curls inward and passes its catch into a long feeding groove.

Much of the animal’s energy comes from symbiotic microbes housed inside that groove. They exploit chemical imbalances between substances rising from the crust and oxidizing compounds produced by radiation in the upper atmosphere. The glassmantle supplies both ingredients by traveling between different layers of the sea.

Its metabolism is slow. A substantial meal may sustain it for weeks. Digestion is less a vigorous furnace than a carefully tended chemical battery.

### Senses without a face

It has no head, but it is not directionless.

A ring of light-sensitive patches around the fan detects the dim sun and the shadows of passing animals. Each trailing ribbon is also a chemical sensor, allowing the glassmantle to distinguish a nutritious plume from a toxic one before its body enters it.

Its finest sense is electrical. Paired organs along its flanks detect tiny disturbances in the conductive ocean. A hidden animal, an approaching predator, or the twitching feeding limbs of another glassmantle all produce recognizable patterns.

To communicate, it releases brief electrical pulses.

A resting group sounds, to a suitable instrument, like scattered raindrops. During courtship, those pulses settle into repeating sequences, answered by neighboring animals after long, deliberate pauses.

### A patient life

Glassmantles reproduce by exchanging packets of hereditary material, then anchoring clusters of dark capsules beneath rock ledges. Each capsule contains a developing juvenile and a starter colony of the microbes it will need to survive.

Development takes years.

The newly emerged animal is no larger than a fingernail. It spends its early life clinging to mineral chimneys, feeding with a tiny fringe of ribbons. Only when its swimming fan has fully unfolded does it release its grip and enter the open sea.

Adults may live for centuries, although much of that time is spent almost motionless in cold, chemically stable depths.

Seen through a submersible’s lights, a gathering of them would resemble a forest of transparent umbrellas suspended in blackness. Then one would fold its fan, another would answer with a faint electrical pulse, and the whole forest would begin, very slowly, to move.
